# The Personal Computer and the New Consumer Monopoly {#sec-4-09}

::: {.chapter-meta}
Act IV — The Silicon Valley Machine · 1975–1985
:::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="draft"}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Pre-Draft Brief

**Core question.** What happens when computing reaches the masses?

**The answer.** The chokepoint moves up a layer. When computing reached
individuals the hardware commoditised almost immediately — and the money went to
whoever controlled the layer above it. Microsoft licensed an operating system to
IBM while retaining the right to license it to everyone else, and that single
contractual reservation was worth more than any factory in the industry.

**The mechanism.** Chokepoint control, relocated. The chapter's argument is that
platform control is the same manoeuvre as Act II ch. 10's move into legal
doctrine: get out of the visible, capital-intensive, competable layer, and into
the invisible one that everything must route through.

**The key fact.** The 1980 IBM agreement was non-exclusive. IBM, the most
powerful computer company in the world, did not insist on exclusivity for the
operating system of its personal computer, and that omission created the
industry's dominant firm.

**The human anchor.** The Xerox PARC demonstration in December 1979, and Steve
Jobs walking out of a building where a corporation had already invented the
future and could not work out what to do with it.

**Excluded voices.** The hardware assembly workforce, increasingly offshore, and
the homebrew culture whose free exchange of designs was enclosed within a few
years — including the open letter about hobbyist copying that announced the
enclosure.

**Proof.** This chapter proves that platform control supersedes hardware by
showing an industry in which the hardware makers competed their margins away
while the operating system licensor took the surplus.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Working summary

The most valuable sentence in the history of software is a clause in a 1980
agreement stating that Microsoft's licence of an operating system to IBM was not
exclusive. IBM, then the most powerful computer company in the world, did not
insist on exclusivity for the operating system of its personal computer. That
omission created the industry's dominant firm.

The chapter builds to it through what came before. The Homebrew Computer Club in
1975 circulated designs freely, and the chapter establishes that as the normal
condition so the reader can see the enclosure when it happens. Apple, founded in
1976, paired Wozniak's engineering with Jobs's insistence that a computer be a
product rather than a kit. And in December 1979 Xerox PARC demonstrated the
graphical interface, the mouse, and networked computing to visitors from Apple —
a corporation that had invented the future and could not work out what a copier
company was supposed to do with it.

Then IBM entered in 1981 with an open architecture built from off-the-shelf
parts, the clone manufacturers arrived, and the hardware commoditised almost
immediately. Margins in assembly collapsed toward nothing while the operating
system licensor took the surplus, and by the early 1990s Windows ran on the
overwhelming majority of personal computers in the world.

The structural argument is that the chokepoint moved up a layer. It is the same
manoeuvre as the Southern Pacific's move into legal doctrine in Act II: get out
of the visible, capital-intensive layer where competitors can reach you, and
into the invisible one that everything must route through. Bayh-Dole passed the
same year as the IBM agreement, and the next chapter takes it up.

The costs are offshore hardware assembly, and the enclosure of a commons — a
transition that was announced at the time, in an open letter complaining that
hobbyists were copying software rather than paying for it.

Never own the layer that can be competed. Own the one everything passes through.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## Beats

1. **Hook.** A non-exclusive clause. The most valuable sentence in the history
   of software, and IBM agreed to it.
2. **The Homebrew Computer Club.** Free circulation of designs, 1975. Establish
   what was normal before it stopped being normal.
3. **Apple, 1976.** Wozniak's engineering and Jobs's positioning. The Apple II
   as the first machine sold as a product rather than a kit.
4. **PARC, December 1979.** What Xerox had — the graphical interface, the mouse,
   networking — and the structural reason a copier company could not
   commercialise it.
5. **IBM enters, 1981.** Open architecture, off-the-shelf parts, and the clone
   industry that follows. Hardware commoditises.
6. **The MS-DOS deal.** The specific terms, the non-exclusivity, and how it
   converted into Windows dominance. Follow the contract, not the personalities.
7. **Bayh-Dole, 1980, noted.** One sentence; ch. 10 does the work.
8. **Where the money ended up.** Sourced margins: assemblers against the
   operating system licensor. The arithmetic is the argument.
9. **The excluded.** Offshore assembly; the enclosure of the hobbyist commons.
10. **Landing.** The lesson relearned every twenty years in this book: never own
   the layer that can be competed. Own the one everything passes through.

:::

::: {.chapter-question}
What happens when computing reaches the masses?
:::

In 1980 IBM licensed an operating system from a small company in Seattle and did
not insist on exclusivity.

That omission — a clause not inserted into a contract by the most powerful
computer company in the world — created the dominant firm of the next thirty
years. It is the most valuable sentence never written in the history of
software, and the chapter opens there because everything else in it follows.

## What was normal before

The Homebrew Computer Club met from March 1975 in Menlo Park, and then in an
auditorium at the Stanford Linear Accelerator Center, and its normal practice
was circulation.

Members brought designs, schematics, and code, and gave them away. The club's
newsletter published circuit diagrams. People copied each other's work and
improved it and brought the improvements back, and the culture of the thing was
closer to an amateur radio society than to an industry.

That is the baseline against which enclosure has to be measured, and it did not
last long. In early 1976 Bill Gates published an open letter to hobbyists
complaining that most users of his BASIC interpreter had not paid for it and
asking who could afford to do professional work for nothing. The letter was
widely resented and it was also correct about the incentive problem, and it
announced the transition from a circulating culture to a licensing one.

## Apple

Apple was founded in 1976 by Steve Wozniak, who designed the machine, and Steve
Jobs, who understood that it should be a product.

The Apple I was a board for people who could solder. The Apple II, in 1977, was
a finished object: a case, a keyboard, a power supply, colour graphics, and
expansion slots. It could be bought by someone who had no intention of building
anything, and it found a business market when VisiCalc — the first spreadsheet —
appeared on it in 1979 and gave people a reason to buy a computer that had
nothing to do with computing.

The Apple II is the moment the personal computer stops being a hobby, and the
crucial decision was packaging rather than engineering.

## PARC

Xerox had established the Palo Alto Research Center in 1970, in the Stanford
Research Park, on Coyote Hill Road.

By the late 1970s PARC had built the Alto: a machine with a bitmapped screen, a
graphical user interface with overlapping windows and icons, a mouse descended
from Engelbart's work at SRI a few miles away, Ethernet networking, a what-you-
see-is-what-you-get editor, and a laser printer. Working, in use internally,
years before anything comparable existed elsewhere.

In December 1979 Xerox permitted Apple engineers to visit, as part of an
arrangement in which Xerox took an equity position in Apple. Jobs saw the
interface and understood immediately what it meant.

The standard telling makes this a theft, and it was not; it was a negotiated
visit, and the ideas were being published and discussed in the research
community anyway. The more interesting question is why Xerox did not
commercialise it, and the answer is structural rather than a failure of vision.
Xerox's business was copiers, sold through a leasing model to corporate
purchasing departments. The Alto cost far too much to make, addressed no market
Xerox served, and would have required the company to build a completely
different sales organisation. The research was superb and the corporation had no
route from it to a product.

Federal and corporate research producing an invention that a different firm
commercialises: it is the Engelbart pattern from chapter 4, repeated four miles
away and a decade later.

## IBM, and the clause

IBM entered the personal computer market in 1981, and it did so in a hurry,
which is why it did everything wrong from its own point of view.

To move fast, the project used off-the-shelf components and published the
technical specifications, so that other companies could build peripherals and
software. And it licensed an operating system from Microsoft rather than
developing one, because developing one would have taken years.

The published architecture allowed Compaq and others to reverse-engineer the
system's firmware and build compatible machines. Hardware competition arrived
immediately and margins collapsed toward the cost of the components, which were
available to everyone.

The operating system did not commoditise, because Microsoft had retained the
right to license MS-DOS to other manufacturers. Every clone maker needed it.
Microsoft sold it to all of them, and then sold Windows to all of them, and by
the early 1990s an operating system from a company with no factories was on the
overwhelming majority of the world's personal computers.

IBM had assumed the value was in the machine. The value was in the layer above
the machine, and it had licensed that layer away non-exclusively in exchange for
a modest per-copy fee.

## The layer that cannot be competed

The structural argument of this chapter is that the chokepoint moved up.

Hardware was the visible, capital-intensive, physically obvious part of the
business, and it was competed to nothing within five years. The operating system
was invisible to the purchaser, cost almost nothing to reproduce, and was
protected by the strongest moat available: every application ran on it, so
switching meant abandoning software you had already bought.

This is the same manoeuvre as the Southern Pacific's move into legal doctrine in
Act II chapter 10, and as the studios' loss of their theatres in the previous
chapter. Get out of the layer a competitor can attack or a court can point at.
Get into the layer everything must route through.

Apple took the other road, integrating hardware and software and keeping both
closed, and spent the following decade losing badly before that strategy became
valuable again under different conditions.

## The story the industry chose

Something else was manufactured in these years alongside the machines, and it is
the story this book has been circling since the Introduction.

Apple's 1984 Super Bowl advertisement presented the personal computer as an
instrument of liberation against a monolithic conformity, with IBM as the
unnamed antagonist. It is one of the most effective pieces of commercial
persuasion ever made, and its argument — that this technology is inherently
democratising and that the people selling it are insurgents — became the
industry's account of itself and has survived every subsequent development.

The counterculture connection was real and is worth stating accurately rather
than dismissing. Stewart Brand's *Whole Earth Catalog*, published from Menlo
Park from 1968, genuinely connected a communitarian, tools-for-independence
sensibility to the emerging computing culture, and a number of the people in the
Homebrew Computer Club came out of it. Brand wrote in 1972 that computers were
coming to the people, and he was right.

The chapter's argument is not that these people were insincere. It is that a
liberation story attached itself to an industry whose structure was becoming, at
exactly that moment, the most concentrated in the American economy. The
advertisement ran in 1984. The operating system monopoly was already forming,
and the men in the garage were on their way to becoming the largest corporations
in the world.

Weber's Protestant merchant believed his prosperity was evidence of election.
The garage founder believes his is evidence of insurgency. Both accounts explain
why the winner deserved to win, and both are held sincerely, which is what makes
them effective.

## Who paid

Two entries for the ledger.

The hardware that commoditised was manufactured by somebody, and increasingly it
was manufactured offshore — the assembly model from chapter 3 extended from
chips to whole machines, through Taiwan, Singapore, Malaysia, and eventually the
Chinese mainland. The falling price of a personal computer is, substantially, a
transfer of the work to people paid less to do it.

And the commons closed. The circulating culture of Homebrew produced the
machines that made the industry, and it was enclosed within about five years by
copyright, licensing, and the ordinary logic of a market. Some of it survived
and regrouped — the free software movement began in 1983 and eventually produced
the operating system that runs most of the world's servers, which is a genuine
counter-example and belongs in the record.

Bayh-Dole passed the same year as the IBM agreement. The next chapter is about
what that did.
